title: The Weather Man
full_review:
It's pretty safe to forecast that when a movie opens with a gloomy shot of undulating ice flows in Lake Michigan canopied by a bleak sky you're not in for a rosy romantic comedy.

Such are the funereal first frames of director Gore Verbinski's "The Weather Man," a dramedy that starts out as simply depressing, but spirals into something more thoroughly cheerless.

Nicolas Cage stars as David Spritz, a popular Chicago TV weatherman trapped in a perfect storm of dejection, desperation and disappointment.

Adding insult to anomie, David is routinely pelted with fast food by "fans" in random drive-bys.

Not even news that he is in the running for a high-profile job on a nationally syndicated morning show seems to shake him out of his melancholy malaise.

While on camera, he's enthusiastic and upbeat, but once the teleprompter turns off so does his smile.

Not that he has much reason to wear one, given the train-wreck state of his personal life including a failed marriage to ex-wife Noreen (Hope Davis) and an estranged relationship with his two troubled children: overweight daughter Shelly (Gemmenne de la Pena) and teenage son Mike (Nicholas Hoult), whose naivete blinds him to his creepy drug counselor's (Gil Bellows) sexual predations.

David wants to patch things up with soon-to-be-remarried Noreen, but she's not interested.

The cherry on David's melted sundae is that his Pulitzer Prize-winning father (played with sullen stoicism by Michael Caine) -- whose approval he badly wants -- is diagnosed with cancer.

To stem David's insecurities and swelling sense of anxiety, he takes up archery, which -- in addition to providing his character with one more eccentric thing to do -- becomes a heavy-handed metaphor for his attempting to achieve his aims but chronically and woefully missing the bull's-eye.

Cage schleps through much of the film wearing a misery-mired expression, but his hangdog performance is oddly sympathetic, and you do want David to get his life together, though he might not necessarily deserve the happiness he seeks.

More light could have been shed on the characters' past relationships, which would have helped viewers understand their present dysfunction.

"The Weather Man" aspires to the sort of angst-chic quirkiness of independent movies by filmmakers such as Charlie Kaufman, David O. Russell and Alexander Payne, but its arrow falls well short of the mark, like those of its sad-sack protagonist.

Though much needed, the humor is, like everything else in the film, dark, and at times lewd.

The film does illustrate the detrimental effect of marital discord on children and manages a few poignantly bittersweet moments, including a life lesson from David's dad that "the right thing and the hard thing are usually the same thing."

Still, with its excessive profanity, shapeless script and trite message that life, like the weather, is highly unpredictable, those little breaks of sunshine are hardly worth suffering through the film's overwhelming cloudiness. Then again, what else could you expect from a movie whose tag line is "bring an umbrella"?

The film contains pervasive rough and sexually explicit language, a sexual encounter with partial nudity, brief violence, an ongoing vulgar gag, a subplot involving abuse of a minor, as well as underage smoking. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
